states.name: New York
states.framework: NYDFS BitLicense / Limited Purpose Trust Charter
states.detail: Most coins commonly called 'stablecoins' count as Virtual Currency under New York's rules, which means issuing one requires a BitLicense or a New York-chartered trust company (the trust route also lets a company handle money transmission and fiduciary duties without extra licenses, which a BitLicense alone doesn't allow). Before issuing, a coin also needs DFS sign-off through self-certification, a spot on DFS's approved 'Greenlist,' or individual approval. Coins already on the Greenlist include Gemini Dollar, Ripple USD, and WisdomTree Dollar.
states.effective: In force since Jun. 8, 2022 guidance
states.sourceText: NY Dept. of Financial Services, Virtual Currency Businesses

states.name: California
states.framework: Digital Financial Assets Law (DFAL)
states.detail: California's Digital Financial Assets Law entered into force on July 1, 2026. Any exchange, custodian, stablecoin issuer, or Bitcoin ATM operator serving California residents must now hold a DFPI license or have filed a complete application, or face civil enforcement of up to $100,000 per day. The law bars licensees from exchanging a stablecoin unless its issuer is licensed, has applied for a license, or is a qualified bank or trust company backing the coin with eligible securities. DFPI expects an initial $100,000 net worth, subject to change, and began accepting applications through NMLS on March 9, 2026.
states.effective: In force since Jul. 1, 2026; DFPI license or complete application now required; enforcement active
states.sourceText: AB 39, Financial Code Div. 1.25

states.name: Texas
states.framework: Money Services Modernization Act (Finance Code Ch. 152)
states.detail: Texas treats qualifying stablecoins as 'money,' which means issuing or transmitting them requires a money transmission license. To count, a stablecoin must be pegged to a currency like the dollar, fully backed by reserve assets, and redeemable for that currency on demand. Licensees must hold a minimum net worth that scales with their size, starting at $100,000. Texas also lets a licensee hold stablecoin itself as part of its required reserves, as long as it's the same stablecoin it owes to customers and is kept in proper custody.
states.effective: In force since Sept. 1, 2023
states.sourceText: Tex. Finance Code Ch. 152, enacted by S.B. 895 (2023)

states.name: Florida
states.framework: Payment Stablecoin Licensing (HB 175) + State Pilot (SB 1568)
states.detail: Florida enacted a package of digital-asset laws signed by Governor DeSantis in late June 2026, all effective immediately. HB 175 requires a money services business to hold a license from the Office of Financial Regulation before issuing a payment stablecoin, with reserves backed one-to-one by cash or similarly safe assets and verified monthly by a CPA, aligning the state framework with the federal GENIUS Act. SB 1568 establishes the Florida Stablecoin Pilot Program, allowing the Department of Financial Services to accept approved payment stablecoins for certain government fees. A companion law, HB 505, requires virtual-currency kiosk operators to register with the OFR.
states.effective: HB 175 and SB 1568 signed by Gov. DeSantis, late Jun. 2026; effective immediately
states.sourceText: Florida House/Senate, HB 175 and SB 1568 bill history

states.name: Wyoming
states.framework: Wyoming Stable Token Act
states.detail: The only state to both regulate and directly issue a stablecoin. The Wyoming Stable Token Commission's Frontier Stable Token (FRNT) can only be backed by cash, US Treasuries maturing within a year, or short-term Treasury repurchase agreements, per W.S. 40-31-106(a). A Trust Account must hold 100% of FRNT's notional value, plus a separate Liquidity Fund Account targeting another 2% as a buffer, with leftover investment earnings flowing quarterly to a state school foundation program. FRNT runs across eight blockchains and went live for public purchase on January 7, 2026, redeemable for $1.00.
states.effective: Mainnet live since Aug. 18, 2025; public purchase since Jan. 7, 2026
states.sourceText: Wyoming Stable Token Commission Factbook

states.name: Illinois
states.framework: Money transmission: Uniform Money Transmission Modernization Act (SB 3412, replacing the Transmitters of Money Act, eff. Jan. 1, 2026). Digital assets/stablecoins: Digital Assets and Consumer Protection Act (DACPA) + Digital Asset Kiosk Act (DAKA)
states.detail: For money transmission generally, Illinois enacted the CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act via SB 3412 (the Uniform Money Transmission Modernization Act, signed August 2024), which replaces the prior Transmitters of Money Act effective January 1, 2026 and adopts NMLS-based multistate licensing. For digital assets specifically, two further laws signed August 18, 2025 (DACPA enacted as Public Act 104-0428) split digital asset oversight in two. DACPA defines a 'digital asset' broadly enough to deliberately capture stablecoins: an asset normally excluded for not being used as an investment loses that exclusion if it's marketed as holding a stable, effectively fixed value, which is exactly how a stablecoin is sold. Businesses must register with IDFPR by July 1, 2027, though customer disclosure and custody protections apply sooner. DAKA separately regulates digital asset kiosks specifically, capping daily transactions at $2,500 for new customers and $10,500 for existing ones, and limiting fees to the greater of $5 or 18% of the transaction.
states.effective: MTMA (SB 3412) money-transmission changes eff. Jan. 1, 2026; DACPA and DAKA eff. Aug. 18, 2025; DACPA registration deadline Jul. 1, 2027
states.sourceText: 205 ILCS 731/ (DACPA) and 205 ILCS 732/ (DAKA); Uniform Money Transmission Modernization Act (SB 3412), amending the Transmitters of Money Act

states.name: Colorado
states.framework: Model Money Transmission Modernization Act (HB 25-1201)
states.detail: Colorado repealed its old Money Transmitters Act and replaced it with the CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act, enabling multistate licensing participation. Unlike Texas, Colorado writes no virtual currency or stablecoin language into the statute at all: 'monetary value' is defined simply as 'a medium of exchange, whether or not redeemable in money,' leaving it to interpretation whether a given stablecoin activity falls within that generic definition. Its net worth formula is identical to Texas's, since both states adopted the same model law: $100,000 or 3% of assets up to $100 million, then a declining percentage above that.
states.effective: Signed Apr. 18, 2025; effective Aug. 6, 2025
states.sourceText: Colorado General Assembly, HB 25-1201

states.name: Washington
states.framework: Uniform Money Services Act
states.detail: Washington's statute defines 'virtual currency' directly and writes it into the definition of 'money transmission' itself, so there's no separate crypto license, just the existing money transmitter framework. Virtual currency licensees face specific disclosure duties: fee schedules, whether funds are insured, a notice that virtual currency transfers are irrevocable, and how errors get resolved. The standard net worth formula (as low as $10,000) jumps to a $100,000 minimum specifically for companies that provide virtual currency storage, though that figure comes from the implementing regulation, not the statute itself.
states.effective: In force

states.name: Arizona
states.framework: CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act (SB 1580, 2022)
states.detail: Arizona replaced its old money transmitter statute with the CSBS model act in 2022 (SB 1580, Chapter 236). Like Colorado, the new statute defines 'monetary value' as simply 'a medium of exchange, whether or not redeemable in money,' with no explicit virtual currency or stablecoin definition. Whether a given stablecoin activity triggers licensing depends on how Arizona DIFI interprets that generic definition. Cryptocurrency kiosk operators face separate, explicit requirements under A.R.S. 6-1236, including daily transaction caps of $2,000 for new customers and $10,500 for existing ones, mandatory fraud warnings, and blockchain analytics requirements. Net worth follows the same formula as Colorado and Texas: $100,000 or 3% of total assets up to $100 million.
states.effective: Signed May 20, 2022
states.sourceText: A.R.S. Title 6, Chapter 12 (SB 1580, Ch. 236, 2022)

states.name: Georgia
states.framework: Georgia Payment Stablecoin Act (HB 1272)
states.detail: Georgia enacted the Georgia Payment Stablecoin Act (HB 1272) in 2026, a dedicated licensing regime for payment stablecoin issuers, but it is not yet in force. Under Section 4, and subject to appropriations by the General Assembly, it becomes effective on the earlier of January 18, 2027 or 120 days after the issuance of final federal GENIUS Act implementing regulations. The Act carves payment stablecoin issuance out of Georgia's existing money transmission laws and authorizes the Department of Banking and Finance to license issuers, on a framework the statute requires to be substantially similar to the GENIUS Act. Licensed issuers must back outstanding stablecoins one-to-one with liquid reserves held in trust for consumers and maintain redemption policies. Beginning July 18, 2028, it becomes unlawful to offer or sell a payment stablecoin in Georgia unless the issuer is a permitted, licensed, or federally qualified issuer. Separately, some virtual-currency money transmission already requires a license under O.C.G.A. Sec. 7-1-680 et seq.
states.effective: Enacted 2026; effective (subject to state appropriations) the earlier of Jan. 18, 2027 or 120 days after federal GENIUS Act final rules; issuer requirement from Jul. 18, 2028
states.sourceText: HB 1272, Georgia Payment Stablecoin Act (as passed House and Senate)

states.name: North Carolina
states.framework: Money Transmitters Act (N.C. Gen. Stat. Ch. 53, Art. 16B)
states.detail: North Carolina regulates stablecoin and virtual-currency activity through its Money Transmitters Act (Chapter 53, Article 16B), administered by the Office of the Commissioner of Banks (NCCOB). The statute expressly defines virtual currency and brings money transmission conducted in whole or in part in virtual currency, including maintaining control of virtual currency on behalf of others, within its licensing requirement. A person engaging in money transmission must obtain a license through NMLS; the license is perpetual but requires an annual NMLS renewal filing. North Carolina does not yet have a dedicated stablecoin-issuer statute. A separate bill, the Virtual Currency Kiosk Consumer Protection Act (HB 920), would place crypto-ATM operators under NCCOB supervision, with implementing rules due by December 1, 2026.
states.effective: Money Transmitters Act in force; virtual currency covered; kiosk bill (HB 920) pending, rules due Dec. 1, 2026
states.sourceText: N.C. Gen. Stat. Ch. 53, Art. 16B (Money Transmitters Act); NC Office of the Commissioner of Banks

states.name: Connecticut
states.framework: Money Transmission Act (virtual currency revisions, PA 25-66 / HB 7082)
states.detail: Connecticut revised its money transmission law to regulate virtual currency, effective October 1, 2025, administered by the Department of Banking. A person engaged in virtual currency business in Connecticut, by receiving, transmitting, storing, or maintaining custody or control of virtual currency, must hold virtual currency of the same type and amount owed or obligated to each customer. Licensees may not lend, hypothecate, pledge, or otherwise use or encumber customer virtual currency without authorization, and the act extends risk-disclosure and receipt requirements to virtual currency transmitters and kiosk operators. Custody may be delegated only to parties qualified to hold it.
states.effective: In force since Oct. 1, 2025
states.sourceText: Conn. Public Act 25-66 (HB 7082); CT Dept. of Banking

states.name: Nevada
states.framework: CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act (NRS Ch. 671, enacted by A.B. 21, 2023); virtual currency covered by FID guidance
states.detail: Nevada enacted the CSBS Model Money Transmission Modernization Act through A.B. 21 (2023), modernizing its money transmission law at NRS Chapter 671, but it did not adopt the model's optional virtual-currency title (Article XIII). NRS Chapter 671 therefore does not expressly mention virtual or digital currency. Instead, the Financial Institutions Division (FID), through published guidance, applies the money-transmission licensing requirement to entities that transmit or hold digital currency, by kiosk, mobile, internet, or other means. Under that guidance, Bitcoin ATM operators must hold a money transmitter license and bond, and licensees holding virtual currency are expected to keep enough of each type to cover outstanding customer obligations. Entities acting purely as digital-asset custodians may instead be regulated as trust companies under NRS Chapter 669. Nevada thus regulates digital assets case by case under its MTMA-based money transmission law rather than a bespoke virtual-currency framework.
states.effective: MTMA enacted via A.B. 21 (2023) at NRS Ch. 671; digital currency covered by FID guidance, not the optional Article XIII virtual-currency title
states.sourceText: NRS Ch. 671, enacted by A.B. 21 (2023) adopting the CSBS Model MTMA without the optional virtual-currency title; digital currency covered by Nevada FID guidance

states.name: Maine
states.framework: Maine Money Transmission Modernization Act (LD 2112)
states.detail: Maine enacted the Maine Money Transmission Modernization Act (LD 2112, signed April 2024), effective August 9, 2024, administered by the Bureau of Consumer Credit Protection. The Act addresses virtual currency: it defines virtual currency and brings 'virtual currency business activity', including exchanging, transferring, or storing virtual currency and virtual currency administration (issuing virtual currency redeemable for money or other value), within its licensing framework. A business engaged in virtual currency business activity in Maine is generally covered.
states.effective: Maine Money Transmission Modernization Act (LD 2112) in force since Aug. 9, 2024; virtual currency business activity covered
states.sourceText: Me. Money Transmission Modernization Act (LD 2112); Maine Bureau of Consumer Credit Protection

states.name: New Hampshire
states.framework: Money Transmission Act (RSA 399-G)
states.detail: New Hampshire requires a money transmitter license under RSA 399-G, administered by the Banking Department, but RSA 399-G:3, VII expressly exempts persons who sell or issue payment instruments or stored value solely in the form of convertible virtual currency, or who receive convertible virtual currency for transmission. The Banking Department confirms it neither licenses nor supervises businesses dealing solely in convertible virtual currency, including a stablecoin. However, money transmitters that handle traditional fiat currency, or that transmit both fiat and cryptocurrency, still must be licensed. Even transactions solely involving cryptocurrency remain subject to New Hampshire's Consumer Protection Act (RSA 358-A), so exemption from licensing is not the same as being unregulated. New Hampshire adopted the virtual-currency exemption in 2017; federal GENIUS Act and FinCEN requirements apply regardless.
states.effective: RSA 399-G:3, VII exempts persons dealing solely in convertible virtual currency from licensing (fiat-touching activity still licensed; RSA 358-A Consumer Protection Act still applies)
states.sourceText: N.H. RSA 399-G:3, VII; N.H. Banking Department position on crypto regulation and jurisdiction

states.name: Rhode Island
states.framework: Currency Transmissions law (R.I. Gen. Laws Ch. 19-14)
states.detail: Rhode Island regulates money transmission under its Currency Transmissions law (R.I. Gen. Laws Title 19, Chapter 19-14), administered by the Department of Business Regulation, and its currency-transmitter licensing applies to virtual currency. H.B. 7282 (2024) added Money Transmission Modernization Act provisions, including tangible-net-worth and permissible-investment requirements and consumer protections, for currency transmitters, including cryptocurrency. Businesses that transmit or hold virtual currency for others are generally covered.
states.effective: Currency Transmissions law (R.I. Gen. Laws Ch. 19-14) in force; applies to virtual currency; MTMA provisions added by H.B. 7282 (2024)
states.sourceText: R.I. Gen. Laws Title 19, Ch. 19-14 (Currency Transmissions); H.B. 7282 (2024); R.I. Department of Business Regulation

states.name: New Jersey
states.framework: Money Transmitters Act (N.J.S.A. 17:15C); Digital Asset & Blockchain Technology Act (A3454, pending)
states.detail: New Jersey's treatment of virtual currency is unsettled. It licenses money transmission under the Money Transmitters Act (N.J.S.A. 17:15C), administered by the Department of Banking and Insurance, and historically regulated crypto firms as money transmitters, but virtual currency does not fit cleanly within the statutory definitions of 'money' or 'payment instrument,' making that application awkward. The Digital Asset and Blockchain Technology Act (A3454) is pending before the legislature (approved in committee, not enacted); if passed, it would move digital-asset licensing to the Bureau of Securities in the Division of Consumer Affairs, clarify that digital assets are not money-transmission instruments, and require a license for digital-asset business activity (custody, trading, transfer). Until then, whether pure virtual currency requires a New Jersey money transmitter license is not firmly settled. Federal GENIUS Act and FinCEN requirements apply regardless.
states.effective: Money Transmitters Act (N.J.S.A. 17:15C) in force but virtual-currency fit is awkward and unsettled; dedicated Digital Asset Business Act (A3454) pending, not enacted
states.sourceText: N.J.S.A. 17:15C; N.J. Dept. of Banking and Insurance; A3454 (pending); N.J. Bureau of Securities

states.name: Delaware
states.framework: Sale of Checks and Transmission of Money Act (5 Del. C. Ch. 23); Money Transmission and Virtual Currency Modernization Act (SB 18, enacted 2026)
states.detail: Delaware currently requires a money transmitter license under its Sale of Checks and Transmission of Money Act (5 Del. C. Chapter 23, Sec. 2303), administered by the Office of the State Bank Commissioner, and applies it to virtual currency transmission in practice, with major digital-asset exchanges holding Delaware money transmitter licenses. In July 2026, Governor Meyer signed Senate Bill 18, the Delaware Money Transmission and Virtual Currency Modernization Act, part of a banking-modernization package aligning Delaware with the federal GENIUS Act. SB 18 replaces Chapter 23 with a comprehensive licensing framework for money transmitters and virtual currency businesses, including stablecoins. It takes effect the earlier of one year after enactment (around July 2027) or when the State Bank Commissioner promulgates final regulations.
states.effective: Sale of Checks Act (Ch. 23) in force and applied to virtual currency; SB 18 signed July 2026, effective the earlier of 1 year after enactment (~July 2027) or upon final regulations
states.sourceText: 5 Del. C. Ch. 23; Del. SB 18 (Money Transmission and Virtual Currency Modernization Act, enacted 2026); Office of the State Bank Commissioner

states.name: Maryland
states.framework: Maryland Money Transmission Act (digital-asset authority via SB 759)
states.detail: Maryland regulates money transmission under the Maryland Money Transmission Act, administered by the Office of the Commissioner of Financial Regulation (OFR). OFR guidance confirms that receiving cryptocurrency from a customer and transferring it constitutes regulated money transmission, so virtual-currency businesses are generally licensed. Senate Bill 759 established explicit statutory authority to regulate digital assets under the Money Transmission Act, effective June 1, 2026. Virtual currency kiosk operators are separately regulated: a final rule effective March 30, 2026 (under Ch. 117 / S.B. 305, 2025) requires kiosk operators and each kiosk to register through NMLS.
states.effective: Money Transmission Act in force (OFR: crypto transmission licensed); digital-asset authority via SB 759 (eff. June 1, 2026); VC kiosk registration rule eff. Mar. 30, 2026
states.sourceText: Maryland Money Transmission Act; SB 759 (2026); Office of the Commissioner of Financial Regulation

states.name: Virginia
states.framework: Money Transmission Modernization Act (HB 1942, Ch. 19.1)
states.detail: Virginia's Money Transmission Modernization Act (HB 1942, enacted in 2025 as Acts of Assembly Chapter 214) takes effect July 1, 2026, replacing Chapter 19 of Title 6.2 with a new Chapter 19.1 administered by the State Corporation Commission's Bureau of Financial Institutions. Under Sec. 6.2-1922, 'money' does not include virtual currency, and because money transmission is defined in terms of money, payment instruments, and stored value, a business engaged solely in transmitting virtual currency, including a stablecoin, generally falls outside the licensing requirement. In practice the exclusion is narrower for stablecoins: activity that also moves fiat currency, such as redemption or on- and off-ramps, transmits 'money' and can still be captured. Federal GENIUS Act and FinCEN requirements apply regardless.
states.effective: MTMA (HB 1942, Acts ch. 214) effective July 1, 2026; virtual currency expressly excluded from 'money' (Sec. 6.2-1922, Ch. 19.1)
states.sourceText: Va. Code Sec. 6.2-1922 (Ch. 19.1, eff. Jul. 1, 2026; HB 1942 / Acts ch. 214); SCC Bureau of Financial Institutions

states.name: South Carolina
states.framework: South Carolina Uniform Money Services Act (Title 35, Ch. 11; adopts the CSBS MTMA); S163 (2026) digital-asset exemptions
states.detail: South Carolina regulates money transmission under the South Carolina Uniform Money Services Act (Title 35, Chapter 11), administered through the Attorney General's Money Services Division. (The chapter, originally the Anti-Money Laundering Act, was renamed by 2024 Act No. 218, effective July 2, 2024, which substantially adopted the CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act without its optional virtual-currency title.) The statute does not expressly address virtual currency, and the Money Services Division's interpretive position is that virtual currency does not, by itself, qualify as 'monetary value,' so virtual currency alone is not money transmission. South Carolina reinforced this by statute in 2026 with S163, which provides that a person exchanging a digital asset for another digital asset without the exchange of legal tender or bank deposits, or engaged in digital-asset mining, node operation, or blockchain software development, is not required to obtain a money transmitter license (S163 also bars state use of a central bank digital currency and protects self-custody). The exclusion remains narrower for stablecoins in practice: activity involving legal tender, such as redemption or on- and off-ramps, falls outside these exemptions and may require a license. Federal GENIUS Act and FinCEN requirements apply regardless.
states.effective: Uniform Money Services Act in force (Division: VC not 'monetary value'); S163 (2026) statutorily exempts crypto-to-crypto without legal tender, mining, nodes, and blockchain development from money-transmitter licensing
states.sourceText: S.C. Code Title 35, Ch. 11 (Uniform Money Services Act); S.C. S163 (2026); Money Services Division

states.name: Massachusetts
states.framework: Money Transmission Law (Ch. 312 of the Acts of 2024; MGL c. 169B)
states.detail: Massachusetts overhauled its money transmission regime with Chapter 312 of the Acts of 2024, codified as MGL c. 169B ('Regulation of Money Transmission') and administered by the Division of Banks. The Division began licensing and regulating money transmitters under c. 169B effective January 1, 2026 (NMLS applications opened around July 1, 2025). The Division has stated that most common transactional virtual currencies, expressly including stablecoins such as USDC, are a form of 'monetary value' under c. 169B, Sec. 1, so virtual-currency transmission requires a license. Non-convertible or closed-loop currencies (for example, in-game currency) are not 'monetary value.' The law is consumer-protection focused, covering money transmission for personal, family, or household purposes.
states.effective: MGL c. 169B (Ch. 312, Acts of 2024); licensing effective Jan. 1, 2026; Division treats transactional virtual currency including USDC as 'monetary value' (licensed)
states.sourceText: Mass. Ch. 312, Acts of 2024 (MGL c. 169B, Sec. 1); Massachusetts Division of Banks FAQs

states.name: Pennsylvania
states.framework: Money Transmission Business Licensing Law, as amended by Act 7 of 2025
states.detail: Pennsylvania regulates money transmission under the Money Transmission Business Licensing Law, administered by the Department of Banking and Securities (DoBS), and virtual currency is now covered by statute. After 2019 DoBS guidance that virtual currency was not 'money' and a 2024 policy statement reversing that view, the legislature enacted Act 7 of 2025, which amended the law to expressly require a license to 'engage in the business of transmitting virtual currency ... for a fee' and retitled it to reference virtual currency. Entities that transmit virtual currency, including stablecoins, for a fee generally must be licensed, subject to exemptions such as transmission solely for personal or household use and certain self-hosted wallet activity. The Act takes effect 60 days after enactment (August 26, 2025), and DoBS rescinded its prior virtual-currency statement of policy. Note that a federally-permitted payment stablecoin issuer (PPSI) is preempted by the GENIUS Act from Pennsylvania's licensing requirement for its stablecoin activity; non-issuer transmitters remain subject to it.
states.effective: Money Transmission Business Licensing Law as amended by Act 7 of 2025; effective 60 days after enactment (Aug. 26, 2025); virtual-currency transmission for a fee licensed by statute
states.sourceText: Pa. Act 7 of 2025 (Money Transmission Business Licensing Law); Pa. Dept. of Banking and Securities

states.name: District of Columbia
states.framework: Money Transmissions Act (D.C. Code Title 26, Ch. 10, Sec. 26-1001)
states.detail: The District of Columbia requires a money transmitter license under its Money Transmissions Act (D.C. Code Title 26, Chapter 10; Sec. 26-1001), administered by the Department of Insurance, Securities and Banking (DISB). By DISB bulletin, and relying on United States v. Harmon (in which the court treated Bitcoin as functioning like money under the District's money-transmission definition), DISB considers Bitcoin and other virtual currency used as a medium of exchange, method of payment, or store of value to be money, so receiving for transmission, storing, or taking custody of virtual currency requires a license. Operating a virtual-currency kiosk or transmitting virtual currency without a license violates Sec. 26-1002 and can carry civil and criminal penalties.
states.effective: Money Transmissions Act (D.C. Code Sec. 26-1001 et seq.) in force; DISB treats virtual currency as money (per bulletin and U.S. v. Harmon); VC transmission/custody licensed
states.sourceText: D.C. Code Title 26, Ch. 10 (Sec. 26-1001 et seq.); DISB cryptocurrency & money transmission bulletin

states.name: Ohio
states.framework: Ohio Money Transmitters Act + DFI Interpretive Guidance 2022-01
states.detail: Ohio's Division of Financial Institutions treats businesses that buy, sell, or transmit cryptocurrency as money transmitters that must be licensed before serving Ohio customers. Interpretive Guidance 2022-01 covers crypto exchanges, kiosks/BTMs, and businesses with independent control over a customer's virtual currency. Stablecoin activity involving transmission or fiat conversion would require licensure on the same basis.
states.effective: Interpretive Guidance 2022-01, effective Aug. 31, 2022
states.sourceText: Ohio Div. of Financial Institutions, Money Transmitters

states.name: Michigan
states.framework: Michigan Money Transmission Services Act (Act 250 of 2006)
states.detail: Michigan's money-transmission law predates crypto and was never updated for it. DIFS's position is that cryptocurrency is not 'money' (not backed by tangible assets or insured deposits), so the pure-crypto leg falls outside DIFS authority. Fiat-to-crypto and crypto-to-fiat transactions do require a money transmitter license, and major exchanges hold Michigan MT licenses. Treatment of stablecoins specifically remains unsettled.
states.effective: Act 250 of 2006 (no crypto-specific amendment)
states.sourceText: Michigan DIFS, Money Transmission Services

states.name: Tennessee
states.framework: Tennessee Money Transmitter Act + TDFI Virtual Currency Guidance
states.detail: TDFI's guidance is that cryptocurrency itself is not 'money,' so holding or transmitting pure virtual currency is not money transmission and the MT license does not cover VC transmission. However, converting crypto to or from sovereign currency through a third-party exchanger or automated machine IS money transmission requiring a license, and TDFI has stated that trade in stablecoins must be licensed as money transmission.
states.effective: TDFI Virtual Currency Guidance
states.sourceText: TN Dept. of Financial Institutions, Virtual Currency Guidance

states.name: Minnesota
states.framework: Minnesota Money Transmission Act (broad 'payment instrument' definition)
states.detail: Minnesota's money-transmission statute does not define 'money' and uses a broad 'payment instrument' definition understood to reach virtual currency, so a money transmitter license is required for VC transmission, and major exchanges hold Minnesota licenses. Treatment applies under the general statute rather than a crypto-specific law.
states.effective: Under existing Money Transmission Act (no separate VC statute confirmed)
states.sourceText: Minnesota Dept. of Commerce, Money Services Business

states.name: Missouri
states.framework: Missouri Sale of Checks Law / money transmission (no VC-specific guidance)
states.detail: Missouri's Division of Finance has not published virtual-currency-specific guidance. A money transmitter (Sale of Checks) license is likely required where fiat currency is involved, and at least one major exchange holds a Missouri Sale of Checks license, but the treatment of pure crypto and stablecoins is unsettled absent specific guidance.
states.effective: No VC-specific guidance issued
states.sourceText: Missouri Division of Finance

states.name: Oregon
states.framework: Oregon Money Transmission Law (ORS 717.205)
states.detail: Oregon requires a money transmission license to conduct a money transmission business (ORS 717.205), and the Division of Financial Regulation applies this to cryptocurrency businesses transmitting value for Oregon customers. Stablecoin transmission and fiat conversion would require licensure on the same basis.
states.effective: Under ORS 717 (money transmission license required)
states.sourceText: Oregon Div. of Financial Regulation, Money Transmitter Licensing

states.name: Indiana
states.framework: Indiana Money Transmission (DFI: VC exchange exempt)
states.detail: The Indiana Department of Financial Institutions has stated that a money transmitter license is not required for a fiat or virtual currency exchange where the consumer is strictly buying or selling currency and cannot send fiat to another consumer. A virtual currency exchange therefore does not generally require an Indiana money transmitter license.
states.effective: Per DFI money transmitter licensing FAQ (NMLS)
states.sourceText: Indiana Dept. of Financial Institutions (money transmitter FAQ)

states.name: Iowa
states.framework: Iowa money transmission + Division of Banking VC guidance
states.detail: Iowa's Division has held that virtual currency qualifies as 'monetary value,' so receiving virtual currency for transmission in Iowa requires a money transmission license, and the Division has issued guidance for virtual currency kiosks. Major exchanges (Coinbase, Binance, Gemini) are registered as money transmitters in Iowa.
states.effective: Per Division of Banking guidance (VC = monetary value)
states.sourceText: Iowa Division of Banking, Guidance for Virtual Currency Kiosks

states.name: Kansas
states.framework: Kansas Money Transmitter Act + OSBC Guidance (MT 2014-01)
states.detail: Kansas OSBC guidance states that an entity engaged solely in the transmission of cryptocurrency is not required to obtain a license, and that exchanging one cryptocurrency for another, or transferring cryptocurrency between accounts, does not by itself qualify as money transmission because crypto is not 'money.' Transactions involving sovereign currency (fiat) can still trigger licensing.
states.effective: OSBC Cryptocurrency Guidance MT 2014-01
states.sourceText: Kansas Office of the State Bank Commissioner, Guidance MT 2014-01

states.name: Kentucky
states.framework: Kentucky money transmission (transmission of money or monetary value)
states.detail: Kentucky requires a license to operate a money transmission business, covering the transmission of money or monetary value by any means, which is understood to reach cryptocurrency businesses transmitting value for Kentucky customers. Treatment applies under the general money transmission statute rather than a crypto-specific law.
states.effective: Under Kentucky money transmission statute
states.sourceText: Kentucky Dept. of Financial Institutions, Money Transmission

states.name: Hawaii
states.framework: Hawaii Money Transmitters Modernization Act (HRS Ch. 489D); virtual currency excluded by DFI interpretation (post Digital Currency Innovation Lab)
states.detail: As of July 1, 2024, Hawaii's Division of Financial Institutions determined that virtual-currency activity is no longer treated as money transmission, so a standalone virtual-currency business (including transmitting or exchanging stablecoins) does not need a Hawaii money transmitter license. This exclusion rests on regulator interpretation following the multi-year Digital Currency Innovation Lab rather than an express statutory carve-out, which makes it less durable, and adding a fiat-currency leg, custody of customer assets, or a virtual-currency kiosk can change the analysis. Federal FinCEN and SEC requirements still apply.
states.effective: DFI determination effective Jul. 1, 2024 (Digital Currency Innovation Lab concluded); interpretation-based, not statutory
states.sourceText: Hawaii DFI / DCCA (Digital Currency Innovation Lab conclusion, eff. Jul. 1 2024); Greenberg Traurig analysis

states.name: Alabama
states.framework: Alabama Monetary Transmission Act (Ala. Code Title 8, Ch. 7A); virtual currency covered as monetary value
states.detail: Alabama licenses money transmission under the Monetary Transmission Act, which covers the transmission of monetary value. The Alabama Securities Commission applies this to virtual currency, so transmitting or exchanging stablecoins on behalf of others generally requires a money transmitter license, with financial requirements including minimum net worth and a surety bond. Whether virtual currency is expressly named or captured by interpretation should be confirmed.
states.effective: Monetary Transmission Act in force; virtual-currency coverage applied by the Alabama Securities Commission
states.sourceText: Alabama Monetary Transmission Act (Ala. Code Title 8, Ch. 7A); Alabama Securities Commission; Carlton Fields 50-state survey

states.name: Alaska
states.framework: Alaska Uniform Money Services Act (fiat only); virtual currency not regulated per Division of Banking & Securities guidance
states.detail: Alaska has no virtual-currency-specific statute. The Division of Banking and Securities has stated it is not authorized under current law to regulate virtual currencies, and that only transactions involving fiat currency fall under the state's Money Transmitter law (the Uniform Money Services Act). Virtual-currency-only activity is therefore not licensed at the state level, but this rests on guidance and prior efforts to bring virtual currency within the money-transmission framework mean pending or future legislation could change it.
states.effective: Guidance-based exclusion; only fiat transactions covered by the Uniform Money Services Act
states.sourceText: Alaska Division of Banking & Securities guidance; Uniform Money Services Act; Carlton Fields 50-state survey

states.name: Arkansas
states.framework: Arkansas Uniform Money Services Act (Ark. Code § 23-55-102, monetary value); Securities Department no-action letters
states.detail: Arkansas has no cryptocurrency-specific statute. Virtual currency may fall within the state's money-transmission law, which covers monetary value defined as a medium of exchange whether or not redeemable in money (Ark. Code § 23-55-102), but the Arkansas Securities Department has issued no-action letters exempting certain digital-asset businesses from licensing. Treatment is therefore unsettled and fact-specific, handled through guidance and no-action relief rather than a clear statutory rule.
states.effective: No crypto-specific statute; treatment via money-services law plus Securities Department no-action letters
states.sourceText: Arkansas Uniform Money Services Act (Ark. Code § 23-55-102); Arkansas Securities Department no-action letters; Carlton Fields survey

states.name: Idaho
states.framework: Idaho Money Transmitters Act (virtual-currency exchangers licensed); Idaho Digital Assets Act
states.detail: The Idaho Department of Finance requires virtual-currency exchangers to hold an Idaho money transmitter license, so transmitting or exchanging stablecoins for customers generally requires licensure. The Department has issued numerous no-action letters exempting businesses that sell their own inventory of digital currency through kiosks. Separately, Idaho's Digital Assets Act categorizes digital assets as intangible personal property and applies existing property law to them.
states.effective: Money Transmitters Act applied to virtual-currency exchangers; Digital Assets Act signed 2025
states.sourceText: Idaho Department of Finance (virtual-currency exchanger licensing); Idaho Digital Assets Act; Astraea state crypto licensing map

states.name: Louisiana
states.framework: Louisiana Virtual Currency Business Act (dedicated virtual-currency license, Office of Financial Institutions)
states.detail: Louisiana enacted the Virtual Currency Business Act, making it one of the few states with a dedicated virtual-currency licensing regime rather than relying solely on general money-transmission law. Engaging in virtual-currency business activity in Louisiana, including transmitting, exchanging, or custodying stablecoins for others, generally requires a virtual-currency license (or money transmitter license) from the Office of Financial Institutions.
